title: Login and single sign-on
like: the "Sign in with" button used by many apps
brief: Employees and customers sign in to many apps through one account. Most of the day is quiet, then 9 am arrives and everyone signs in at once. Attackers also hammer the login with stolen passwords. Let real people in quickly and keep the rest out.

clarify.q: Do apps check a session on every click?
clarify.a: Yes, so session checks are far more common than logins. They must be fast.

clarify.q: Can a session check be a few seconds old?
clarify.a: Yes, if someone signs out, a few seconds of delay is acceptable. A password change must take effect soon.
Limit attempts per account and per address, and log every attempt for audit.

notes: Use the peak and request mix to split sign-ins from session checks.
A password check is deliberately slow and costs real compute.

numbers.label: Session checks per second at peak
Audit log a day
numbers.how: About 150 million events × about 150 bytes ≈ 22 GB (approx.)

hints: Signing in is rare and heavy. Checking a session is frequent and light. Should they take the same path?
Keep sessions in a fast store so a check never touches the password database. Put a rate limiter and a firewall in front of the login.
Capacity does not distinguish attackers from users; account-only hard lockouts can themselves become an attack. Measure the failed boundary, waiting time and retry work before choosing a change.

editorial.summary: Split the cheap, constant session check from the costly, rare sign-in. Sessions live in a key-value store so apps get a fast answer. The identity provider handles password work behind a firewall and a rate limiter, and every attempt goes to an audit log.

designs.name: Fast sessions, guarded sign-in, audit trail
designs.why: A session check reads one key and never reaches the password database. The sign-in path is guarded twice, by the firewall and by per-account limits, and the audit log records each attempt.

tradeoffs: Session checks served from a fast store are quick, but a signed-out session may linger for a few seconds.
Strict attempt limits stop guessing, but can lock out a real user whose account is being attacked.
Long sessions are friendlier, but a stolen session lasts longer. Many teams use short sessions with a refresh.
If login goes down, every connected app goes down with it. That is why it gets the highest uptime target here.
editorial.realWorld: A large company sign-in service handles thousands of session checks for each real sign-in, and sees its peak in the first minutes of the work day (approx.).

correctness.prompt: Login and single sign-on: which invariant does this trace protect, and what failure would break it?
correctness.discussion: Validate and revoke sessions without turning every click into a fragile login. A valid signature does not make an expired or wrong-audience token usable. State the revocation delay. Cached sessions trade availability and speed for a bounded security window. Capacity does not distinguish attackers from users; account-only hard lockouts can themselves become an attack.

fields.label: Step 1. A signed session token arrives with an expired timestamp. Accept it?
options: Reject it after signature, issuer, audience and expiry validation
fields.explanation: A valid signature does not make an expired or wrong-audience token usable.

fields.label: Step 2. A user signs out while a session cache is warm. What is promised?
options: Keep accepting until an arbitrary cache eviction
Bound cached validity and propagate revocation or check a session version
fields.explanation: State the revocation delay. Cached sessions trade availability and speed for a bounded security window.

fields.label: Step 3. One account receives a password-guessing flood. How do you respond?
options: Limit by account and source, with recovery and measured false lockouts
fields.explanation: Capacity does not distinguish attackers from users; account-only hard lockouts can themselves become an attack.

correctness.responsibility: Validate and revoke sessions without turning every click into a fragile login.
correctness.limits: The traffic model does not execute this protocol. The checked trace covers its central responsibility; the written explanation is retained for review.

twist.brief: Demand has settled at about 1500 requests/s. The new monthly ceiling is $48921. The original burst reserve now competes with the operating budget. Decide which reserve to keep, then test its failure headroom. All data and recovery promises still apply.

design.name: Smaller workload, measured reserve
design.why: Reduce the paid floor for the quieter workload, preserving the required copies and recovery settings. This design was checked through the full event day.
